EWORD

9.1 This Indian Standard ( Part `II ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 20 August 1979, after the draft' finalized by the Textile Mill Leather Articles Sectional .Committee had been approved by the Textile Division Council. " 9.2 The Committee responsible for the formulation of ,this standard is of the view that hairly picking bands have become out of use;.therefore, this standard does not contain provisions,related to such bands. 9.9 To familiarize the industry with International System ( S[ ) units, the basic SI units as well as the recommended SI' units for use i,n the textile industry are given in Appendix A. 0.3.1 The Standards of Weights and Measures Act, 1976 also stipulates use of SI units. r<:

I.. SCOPE 1.1 This'standard ( Part I1 ) covers recommendations on storage and, use ofleather picking bands including those used in jute mills. 2. RECOMMENDATIONS ON STORAGE

2.1 The picking bands should be kept inside polyethylene bags and stored in a cool and dry place to ensure that they remain pliable. ( A stiff picking band springs off the pin on the picking stick resulting in uneven picking. ) 2.2 To avoid fungus problem in the storage of vegetable-tanned leather products, use of p-nitrophenol during tanning is recommended; in the case of chrome-tanning this problem does not arise. 3

IS t 9244 ( Part II ) - 1979 3. RECOMMENDATIONS ENSURE OPTIMUM ON USAGE AND MAINTENANCE LIFE OF PICKING BANDS TO

3.1 The picking band has to be of good quality and proper length, never Proper fitting of the pickers to the spindie and proper too short. functioning of the picker gear is important for smooth movement of the pickers. 3.2 A rough surface of the picking stick at the delivery end causes Picking sticks should, therefore, be severe damage to the picking band. checked occasionally for any wear, especially near the delivery end. 3.3 The picker slot, through which the picking band is fastened to the a new picker, should not have sharp edges. While commissioning picker, the edges should be rounded. 3.4 The picking band should be secured to the picker by means of a wooden peg. The hole for inserting the peg should be previously punched and the slitting of the band to insert the peg avoided. 3.5 The length of the picking band between the picker stick should be so adjusted that when the loom is at picker moves freely inward and outward on the When the picking stick is at the innermost position, the the picker and the buffer should be about 6 cm. 3.6 A full-length picking band gives longer life than Butt length should be preferred to cut length. bands. and the picking back centre, the picking spindle. distance between two half-length

NOTE - The thicker butt portion goes on the picker and the other portion goes on the picking stick. The butt portion is longer lasting. By cutting the picking band in two pieces an advantage lies in its having two longer lasting portions from one picking band Further, piece; if one single length is used, this advantage is availed of only once. in a longer .length picking band the portion on the picking sticks ( which is subject to constant frictional contact ) loses its useful properties of elasticity, strength, etc, when it gets the chance to perform at the picking band slot on the picker.

3.7 The picking band should be tied to the picker at its butt end and to the picking stick at its shoulder end in order to ensure longer life. 3.8 For convenience of recognition, the butt and the shoulder ends should be distinctly marked, for example, the butt end may carry two punch marks while the shoulder end may carry a cross. 38.1 The butt and the shoulder ends could be marked for full-length picking bands. But for bands that have to be cut into two, they should be embossed with their brand name on two shoulder ends. Thus, after cutting the band into two pieces, the portion with the brand name goes to the picking stick and the other portion ( butt ) goes to the picker. 3.9 The picking band should not strike against the reed cap, buffer edge or heald staves. 4
